description.en: The Amazon River, river pollution, mountains and maps, how mountains form, the growth of cities and capital cities.

html.en: The Amazon is the largest river in the world by the amount of water it carries, and the second longest river after the Nile. It flows across South America from the Andes Mountains in Peru to the Atlantic Ocean in Brazil.

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth
South America · the biggest river on Earth

rows.en: High in the Andes Mountains, in Peru
The Atlantic Ocean, near the city of Belém, Brazil
From west to east — down from high ground to low ground
About 6,400 km (around 4,000 miles) — the 2nd longest river in the world
Peru → Colombia → Brazil (its basin also reaches Bolivia, Ecuador, Venezuela and Guyana)
It carries more water than any other river — about one fifth (20%) of all the fresh water that flows into the world's oceans
More than 1,000. The biggest are the Madeira, the Rio Negro, the Purús and the Japurá

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth

html.en:
🌴 The Amazon Rainforest

  • The land drained by the river is called the Amazon basin — about 7 million km², mostly covered by the Amazon Rainforest, the largest rainforest on Earth.
  • More than one third of all the known species in the world live there.
  • It is often called the "lungs of the planet" because the trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.
  • Animals: pink river dolphin, piranha, arapaima, anaconda, jaguar, macaw, sloth, caiman. There are over 5,600 known species of fish, and about 50 new ones are found every year.

🚢 Why the river matters to people

  • Water for drinking and for irrigation (watering crops).
  • Transport — there are almost no roads, so the river is the road. Large ocean ships can sail 1,600 km inland to Manaus in Brazil; smaller boats reach Iquitos in Peru.
  • Food — fishing feeds millions of people.
  • Homes for indigenous peoples who have lived along the river for thousands of years.

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth

html.en:
Two facts that always impress an examiner:
① There is no bridge across the main Amazon River — it runs through rainforest where there are almost no roads.
② At Manaus the dark water of the Rio Negro and the sandy water of the Solimões flow side by side without mixing for several kilometres. It is called the Meeting of the Waters.

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth

html.en: Dangers to the Amazon: deforestation (cutting down the rainforest for farms, cattle and timber), mining (which puts mercury into the water), oil spills, and pollution from towns along the banks.

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth

html.en: 🗣️ Say it like this in the exam

source.note: South America · the biggest river on Earth

html.en: "The Amazon River begins as a small stream high in the Andes Mountains of Peru and flows east for about 6,400 km across Brazil until it reaches its mouth at the Atlantic Ocean. It is the largest river in the world by volume because more than 1,000 tributaries join it, and it flows through the Amazon Rainforest, the largest rainforest on Earth."

html.en: Pollution is the contamination of air, water or soil by substances that are harmful to living organisms. It can happen naturally (for example a volcanic eruption) or because of human activities (spilling oil, dumping industrial waste).

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en: Many villages, towns and cities were built near rivers so that people could use the water. Unfortunately, the water that people return to the river after they have used it often contains harmful substances that pollute the river.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en:
1️⃣ The 4 causes of river pollution

  1. Untreated sewage from homes, schools and factories.
  2. Chemical wastes from factories and mines.
  3. Farm chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides.
  4. Waste oil and rubbish.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en: All these different pollutants kill plants and animals and make the water unsafe for people to use.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en:
🟢 Why does a polluted river turn green?

Fertiliser from a farm on the riverbank washes into the water. Tiny plants called algae grow and multiply very fast because of it. When the algae die they sink to the bottom and rot away, and rotting uses up most of the oxygen in the water. That leaves little oxygen for the other water plants and animals — so they die.

2️⃣ Acid rain — the full story

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

rows.en: Fuels such as coal, oil and petrol are burned in factories, power stations and motor vehicles.
They release sulphur dioxide and other gases into the air.
These gases dissolve in droplets of moisture in the atmosphere.
The acid rain falls to the ground — sometimes hundreds of kilometres from where the gases were released.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en:
3️⃣ The damage acid rain does

  • Kills fish and other wildlife in rivers and lakes.
  • Kills trees.
  • Damages crops.
  • Erodes stone buildings and statues.

4️⃣ Preventing river pollution

  • Having strict laws that make it illegal to pollute rivers.
  • Making factories remove harmful substances from their wastewater before they let it flow into rivers.
  • Making factories and mines pay to clean up rivers if they pollute them.
  • Treating sewage to make it safe before the wastewater is returned to a river.
  • Having laws to reduce air pollution from factories, power stations and motor vehicles, in order to reduce acid rain.

5️⃣ The types of pollution — describe each one

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

rows.en: Harmful gases and smoke released into the air by factories, power stations and vehicles. Causes acid rain and breathing problems.
Harmful substances — sewage, chemicals, oil, rubbish — put into rivers, lakes and seas. Kills fish and makes water unsafe to drink.
Rubbish, plastic and chemicals dumped on the ground. It damages the soil so plants cannot grow well.
Unwanted loud sound from traffic, aeroplanes, factories or music. It disturbs people and animals.
Too much artificial light at night from cities. It hides the stars and confuses nocturnal animals.
Hot water released from power stations into rivers. Warm water holds less oxygen, so fish die.
Dangerous radiation escaping from nuclear power stations or waste. It is harmful to all living things.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en:
🇬🇧 Case study: the River Thames

The River Thames has always supplied most of London's water. But by the late 1950s it was so polluted that it was black in colour and it smelled very bad. The main causes were sewage allowed to flow straight into the river and oil from ships using it.

Today it is much cleaner, for two main reasons:

  1. London's old docks were closed because large modern ships could not use them. A new port was built near the mouth of the river where it is deeper and wider.
  2. New sewage works were built, and all wastewater from homes, businesses and factories now has to be treated instead of going straight into the river.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

html.en: Now birds, fish and other wildlife are returning to the Thames. Clean rivers matter because they show the environment is healthy — and because the river water we pollute today may be the water we have to drink tomorrow.

source.note: Polluted rivers · pages 18–19 + the class presentation

  • Ganges — India

html.en: The 300 metre rule. Mountains and hills are both areas of high ground. If the ground rises more than 300 metres above the land around it, it is a mountain. If it rises less than 300 metres, it is a hill.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet
Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

rows.en: The natural features of the land — hills, mountains, lakes and rivers — as well as things made by people, such as roads and towns. Many atlases contain topographic maps.
Only how high the different parts of a region, country or continent are. Nothing else.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en: Memory trick: Topographic = Total picture (nature + people). Relief = Rise of the land only.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en:
🎨 How height is shown with colour

  • On both topographic and relief maps, height is shown using different colours, usually shades of brown and green.
  • All land areas of the same height above sea level are given the same colour.
  • The map needs a key to show what the different colours mean. That is what a map key is for — it explains what every colour and symbol on the map stands for, so you can read it.

🌊 Heights above sea level

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en: Heights and depths on a map are measured above and below the average level of the sea. When we say Mount Everest, the highest mountain in the world, is 8,863 metres high, we mean its height measures 8,863 metres above sea level.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en:
〰️ Contour lines

  • Contour lines are lines joining places that are the same height above sea level.
  • They are exactly level.
  • They do not cross each other. If they seem to join up or stop, it is because they have reached a cliff or some other vertical surface.

📐 Scale — and what it does to the contours

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet
Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en:
Reading the slope from the contour lines:
Contour lines close together → a steep slope.
Contour lines further apart → a gentle slope.
No contour lines at all → the land is flat.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en:
In the large-scale map of Scotland in your book you can see Ben Nevis, Fort William, Loch Linnhe and the rivers Nevis, Kiachnish, Scaddle and Cona. The contour lines are packed tightly around Ben Nevis, so that land is very steep and high.

🌊 River words you must know

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

rows.en: The beginning of a river, usually on high ground.
Smaller rivers that join the main river and make it bigger.
The path the river flows in.
When, after heavy rain, the river overflows its banks.
Where a river flows very fast over rocks — dangerous for boats.
Where a river flows over a cliff.
The end of the river, where it meets a lake or an ocean.
Low, watery land formed at the mouth of a river.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en: Full sentence: "A river is a body of water that flows from high ground to low ground. It begins at the source, is joined by tributaries, flows in its channel between its banks, and ends at its mouth where it meets a lake or an ocean."

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet
Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

rows.en: High, with a peak, made of rock and soil, sometimes with snow at the top.
A mound of raised land that is smaller than a mountain.
A narrow valley with steep sides caused by erosion.
A high, steep slope of rock or soil, usually along an ocean or sea.
A large area of flat land that is raised higher than the land around it.
Flat land beside a river that floods when the river rises.
A strip of land that extends out into a body of water.
A narrow strip of land connecting two larger areas of land.
Low, watery land formed at the mouth of a river.
A pile of sand created by the waves or the wind.
A hollow space in the ground or a mountain with an opening.
One of the seven largest bodies of land on Earth.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en: 💧 Bonus from the booklet: the water cycle

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

rows.en: The sun warms the water and it turns into a gas (water vapour) that rises from land, rivers and oceans.
Water vapour released from living things — plants, trees, animals and people.
High in the sky the vapour gets cold, turns back into water droplets and forms clouds.
The clouds get full and heavy, and the water falls as rain, hail or snow.
The rain flows over the land back into creeks, rivers and oceans.
The water collects and is stored in oceans, lakes and rivers — and the cycle starts again.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en: Earth's spheres: geosphere = land · atmosphere = air · hydrosphere = water · biosphere = living things.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet
Mountains unit · pages 20–21 + the map booklet

html.en:
Question 1 answer, ready to write:
Two types of mountain are fold mountains (examples: the Himalayas, the Alps, the Andes — also the Rockies and the Urals) and block mountains (examples: the highland areas of East Africa, such as the Ruwenzori, the Usambara and the Uluguru mountains). A third type is volcanic mountains (examples: Mount Kilimanjaro, Fujiyama, Mount Taranaki).

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en:
🗻 Alone or in a chain?

  • A few mountains stand alone: Fujiyama in Japan, Mount Taranaki in New Zealand, Mount Kenya in Africa, and Mount Kilimanjaro in Africa (a volcanic mountain that stands alone).
  • Most mountains are found in long chains called ranges. Examples of mountain ranges: the Alps, the Andes, the Himalayas, the Sarawat and the Rocky Mountains.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en: Definition to learn: a mountain range is a long chain of mountains joined together.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en:
🌍 What is the Earth made up of?

  • The Earth is made up of layers of rock.
  • The solid outside layer of rock is called the Earth's crust.
  • Beneath the crust is a layer called the mantle.
  • Near the top of the mantle some of the rocks are so hot that they have melted to form a thick liquid, like sticky tar — this is magma (molten rock).

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en: What is the Earth's crust made up of? The crust is made up of large pieces called plates, which fit together like the pieces of a jigsaw puzzle. Some plates carry continents and others carry oceans. The plates move slowly, floating on the molten rock of the mantle below them.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en:
🌋 Volcanic mountains

  1. All the rocks around the mantle press down on it, so the molten rock is under great pressure.
  2. If there is a weak point in the Earth's crust, the molten rock bursts through it…
  3. …and out on to the Earth's surface, forming a volcano.
  4. The material builds up around the opening and forms a volcanic mountain.

Example: Mount Kilimanjaro in Africa is a volcanic mountain that stands alone.

🗻 Fold mountains

  1. The crust is made of plates that move slowly on the molten rock of the mantle.
  2. Where two plates push against each other, the Earth's crust is slowly pushed up into folds or ridges.
  3. These folds form fold mountains.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en: The Himalayas story — learn this example. India used to be a long way from Asia. Slowly the plate with India on it moved closer to the plate with Asia on it. The rocks in the sea between them were gradually pushed up into folds that now form the Himalayan mountain range. That is why it is sometimes possible to find fossilised seashells near the tops of the Himalayas. 🐚

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en:
Many other ranges — the Alps, Rockies, Andes and Urals — are also fold mountains.

🧱 Faults and block mountains

  1. While some plates are pushing together, others are moving apart. Europe and North America are slowly moving further apart — each year the Atlantic Ocean is a few centimetres wider.
  2. As the rocks move apart they often crack and create breaks called faults.
  3. Sometimes large blocks of rock are pushed up between two faults.
  4. These blocks may be so large and high that they form block mountains — like some of the highland areas of East Africa.
  5. Block mountains often have flat tops. A flat-topped highland is called a plateau.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en:
Do not mix these up!
Plates PUSH TOGETHER → the crust folds → FOLD mountains.
Plates MOVE APART → the rock cracks into faults → blocks pushed up → BLOCK mountains.
Magma BURSTS THROUGH a weak point → VOLCANIC mountains.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23
Mountains unit · pages 22–23

rows.en: 1. Name 2 types of mountains and give 3 examples of each
Fold mountains — Himalayas, Alps, Andes. Block mountains — the highland areas of East Africa (Ruwenzori, Usambara, Uluguru). (A third type is volcanic: Kilimanjaro, Fujiyama, Mount Taranaki.)
2. What is the Earth made up of?
Layers of rock. The solid outside layer is the crust; beneath it is the mantle, where some rock is melted into a thick liquid like sticky tar.
The rocks around the mantle press down, so the molten rock is under great pressure. Where there is a weak point in the crust, the molten rock bursts through on to the surface, forming a volcano.
Long chains of mountains. Examples: the Alps, Andes, Himalayas, Sarawat and Rocky Mountains.
Where two plates push against each other, the Earth's crust is slowly pushed up in folds or ridges, forming fold mountains.
When plates move apart, the rocks crack and create faults. Large blocks of rock are pushed up between two faults, forming block mountains — often with flat tops (plateaus).
7. What is the Earth's crust made up of?
Large pieces called plates, which fit together like a jigsaw puzzle. Some carry continents, some carry oceans, and they all move slowly on the molten rock below.

source.note: Mountains unit · pages 22–23

html.en: Where did the first cities develop? The first cities grew up about 5,000 to 6,000 years ago, in Mesopotamia — the land between the rivers Tigris and Euphrates (in modern Iraq). Other early cities appeared along the Nile in Egypt, the Indus in Pakistan/India, and the Yellow River in China. They all grew next to rivers, because rivers gave people water, food, fertile soil for farming and transport.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en:
🏢 What is a modern city?

A modern city is a very large settlement where a lot of people live and work. In most modern cities the land is used for:

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations
Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en:
• schools
  • hospitals
  • railway and bus stations
  • civic buildings, such as city halls or town halls

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en: Many cities have a mixture of older and newer buildings, because the city has developed over a long period of time.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en: 🏗️ Why are skyscrapers built in city centres?

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en: Because land in the city centre is very expensive. To make the most of the land, people build very tall buildings called skyscrapers, which tower over the older buildings. Building upwards fits far more offices and homes onto a small, costly piece of ground.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en:
🏦 City zones and the CBD

  • Cities may be divided into different areas or zones, each with a different purpose.
  • The middle of the city is called the central business district (CBD).
  • In the CBD you find most of the offices, banks, large shops, art galleries and museums.

🚆 How transport helped cities grow outwards

  1. Better transport — commuter trains and metros — helps cities spread outwards.
  2. More people can then live further away from the city centre and still be able to travel to work.
  3. As a result, new residential areas called suburbs develop around the edges of the city.

🔑 Key words

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

rows.en: The centre of the city, where most businesses are located.
A person who travels from home to work.
Areas on the edge of the city where people live.
One very large urban area formed when neighbouring towns and cities merge together.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en:
🏘️ Conurbations

As cities grow, they spread out into the surrounding countryside. Eventually neighbouring towns and cities may merge and become one very large urban area. This is called a conurbation.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

rows.en: Originally about 13 kilometres apart. Over time, as both cities grew, they joined to form one conurbation.
Joined into one very large conurbation. Most people agree this is the largest conurbation in the world, with 34 million people living there.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en: Did you know? Sydney and Melbourne are the two largest cities in Australia. In the nineteenth century they were planned and built as important cities.

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en: 🤔 Think about it: living in a conurbation

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

rows.en: More jobs · more shops, schools and hospitals · better public transport · lots to do
Traffic jams and air pollution · expensive housing · crowded · very little countryside or green space left

source.note: Modern cities · city zones · conurbations
Modern cities · city zones · conurbations

html.en:
What is a capital city, and what is its main purpose?
Every country has a capital city. It is where the government of the country meets. The capital city is usually the largest and most important city in a country. Its main purpose is to be the centre of government — where the country's laws are made and where the leaders work.

source.note: Definition + South America, North America and Europe

html.en:
🏗️ Capital cities that were built on purpose

Some countries build their capital cities specially. For example, in the nineteenth century, Sydney and Melbourne were planned and built as important cities.

source.note: Definition + South America, North America and Europe

html.en: Canberra, Australia — the story the exam likes. The people could not decide whether Sydney or Melbourne should be the capital city of Australia. So they built a new city, called Canberra, to be the capital. Canberra is inland, about halfway between Sydney and Melbourne. In 1927 it became Australia's capital.

source.note: Definition + South America, North America and Europe
Definition + South America, North America and Europe

html.en: This is why "the capital is always the biggest city" is wrong. Canberra, Brasília and Abuja are not the biggest cities in their countries — but they are where the government meets.

source.note: Definition + South America, North America and Europe
Definition + South America, North America and Europe
Definition + South America, North America and Europe

stem.en: On which continent is the Amazon River?

solution.en: South America.

html.en: High in the Andes Mountains in Peru

stem.en: Where is the source of the Amazon River?

solution.en: The source is high in the Andes Mountains of Peru. The source is always the beginning of a river.

stem.en: Where is the mouth of the Amazon River?

solution.en: The Atlantic Ocean, near Belém in Brazil. The mouth is where a river meets a lake or an ocean.

stem.en: In which direction does the Amazon flow?

solution.en: West to east — from the Andes in the west, across the continent, to the Atlantic in the east.

stem.en: About how long is the Amazon River?

solution.en: About 6,400 km (roughly 4,000 miles).

stem.en: Which river is the longest in the world?

solution.en: The Nile is the longest. The Amazon is the second longest — but it is first for the amount of water it carries.

html.en: Because it carries more water than any other river
Because it has the most bridges

stem.en: Why is the Amazon called the largest river in the world?

solution.en: It carries more water than any other river — about one fifth of all the fresh water flowing into the world's oceans.

stem.en: The three main countries the Amazon flows through are…

solution.en: Peru → Colombia → Brazil.

html.en: A smaller river that joins a bigger river

stem.en: What is a tributary?

solution.en: A smaller river that joins the main river and makes it bigger. The Amazon has more than 1,000.

stem.en: Which of these is a major tributary of the Amazon?

solution.en: The Rio Negro. Others are the Madeira, the Purús and the Japurá.

stem.en: The huge forest around the river is…

solution.en: The Amazon Rainforest — the largest rainforest on Earth, home to more than a third of all known species.

html.en: Because the trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen
Because it is full of birds
Because the wind is strong there

stem.en: Why is the Amazon Rainforest called the "lungs of the planet"?

solution.en: The trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen.

stem.en: Which animal lives in the Amazon River itself?

solution.en: The pink river dolphin. Also piranhas, arapaima and caimans.

html.en: It runs through rainforest where there are almost no roads

stem.en: Why are there almost no bridges across the main Amazon River?

solution.en: It flows through remote rainforest with almost no roads, so a bridge would lead nowhere.

stem.en: How do most people and goods travel in the Amazon region?

solution.en: By boat. The river is the road — ocean ships can even reach Manaus, 1,600 km inland.

html.en: Where two rivers of different colours flow side by side without mixing

stem.en: What is the Meeting of the Waters at Manaus?

solution.en: The dark Rio Negro and the sandy Solimões flow side by side without mixing for several kilometres.

stem.en: Which is the biggest threat to the Amazon Rainforest?

solution.en: Deforestation — cutting down the forest for farms, cattle and timber. Mining and pollution are threats too.

stem.en: Which mountain range is the Amazon's source in?

solution.en: The Andes, which run down the western side of South America.

stem.en: About what fraction of the fresh water flowing into the world's oceans comes from the Amazon?

solution.en: About one fifth (20%).

html.en: Water for drinking and irrigation, and routes for transport by boat

stem.en: Rivers were important to people in the past mainly because they provided…

solution.en: Water for drinking and irrigation, and they were important routes for transport by boat.

html.en: The contamination of air, water or soil by substances harmful to living organisms

stem.en: What is pollution?

solution.en: The contamination of air, water or soil by substances that are harmful to living organisms.

html.en: Naturally, such as through volcanic eruptions, and because of human activities

stem.en: Pollution can happen…

solution.en: Both. Naturally (volcanic eruptions) and through human activities (oil spills, industrial waste).

html.en: So people could make use of the water

stem.en: Why were so many villages, towns and cities built near rivers?

solution.en: So that people could make use of the water. The problem is what they return to the river afterwards.

html.en: Chemical wastes from factories and mines
Farm chemicals such as fertilisers and pesticides

stem.en: Which of these is not one of the four causes of river pollution in your book?

solution.en: The four are untreated sewage · chemical wastes · farm chemicals · waste oil and rubbish.

stem.en: Untreated sewage comes from…

solution.en: Homes, schools and factories.

stem.en: Farm chemicals that pollute rivers are…

solution.en: Fertilisers and pesticides.

html.en: Because of the reflection of the trees
Because it is filled with tiny plants called algae
Because of green paint from factories
Because of the colour of the riverbed

stem.en: Why does a polluted river sometimes look green?

solution.en: It is filled with algae, which grow very fast because of fertiliser washed off a farm.

html.en: When the algae die and rot they use up most of the oxygen in the water
The algae make the water too cold
The algae block the sunlight only

stem.en: Why do fish die in a river full of algae?

solution.en: The dead algae sink and rot, using up most of the oxygen, so there is little oxygen left for other plants and animals.

stem.en: Which fuels produce the gases that cause acid rain?

solution.en: Coal, oil and petrol, burned in factories, power stations and motor vehicles.

stem.en: Which gas is named in your book as the main cause of acid rain?

solution.en: Sulphur dioxide (and other gases).

html.en: The gases dissolve in droplets of moisture in the atmosphere
The rain falls through smoke on the ground
Factories pour acid into the clouds
The sun heats the sea too much

stem.en: How does acid rain actually form?

solution.en: The gases dissolve in droplets of moisture in the atmosphere and form droplets of acid rain.

html.en: Sometimes hundreds of kilometres from where the gases were released

stem.en: Where does acid rain fall?

solution.en: Sometimes hundreds of kilometres away — which is why acid rain is an international problem.

html.en: It kills fish and wildlife in rivers and lakes
It kills trees and damages crops

stem.en: Which of these is not a damage caused by acid rain?

solution.en: The damages are: kills fish and wildlife, kills trees, damages crops, erodes stone buildings.

html.en: Laws to reduce air pollution from factories, power stations and motor vehicles

stem.en: A good way to reduce acid rain is…

solution.en: Reduce the air pollution at the source, and there are fewer gases to make acid rain.

html.en: Remove the harmful substances from it

stem.en: What should factories do with their wastewater before it goes into a river?

solution.en: Remove harmful substances from it first.

html.en: Make them pay to clean the river up

stem.en: If a factory or mine pollutes a river, one way to prevent it happening again is…

solution.en: Making factories and mines pay to clean up rivers if they pollute them.

stem.en: What is done to sewage so it is safe to return to a river?

solution.en: It is treated to make it safe before the wastewater is returned to the river.

html.en: Black in colour and it smelled very bad

stem.en: By the late 1950s the River Thames was…

solution.en: Black and smelly. The main causes were sewage flowing straight into it and oil from ships.

html.en: The old docks were closed and a new port was built near the mouth of the river

stem.en: One reason the Thames is cleaner today is that…

solution.en: The old docks closed (large modern ships could not use them) and a new port was built near the mouth, where the river is deeper and wider.

html.en: New sewage works — all wastewater now has to be treated

stem.en: The other main reason the Thames is cleaner is…

solution.en: New sewage works were built, and all wastewater from homes, businesses and factories has to be treated.

stem.en: Which river supplies most people in Pakistan with their water and is heavily polluted by factory chemicals?

solution.en: The River Indus.

html.en: Hot water released into a river, which holds less oxygen so fish die

stem.en: Thermal pollution is…

solution.en: Hot water released into rivers. Warm water holds less oxygen, so fish die.

html.en: Unwanted loud sound from traffic, aeroplanes or factories

stem.en: Noise pollution is…

solution.en: Unwanted loud sound that disturbs people and animals.

html.en: Because rivers look nicer when clean
Because the river water we pollute today may be the water we have to drink tomorrow

stem.en: The best final sentence for "why should we not pollute rivers?" is…

solution.en: Straight from your book — the water we pollute today may be the water we drink tomorrow.

stem.en: The ground rises 420 metres above the land around it. It is a…

solution.en: More than 300 m → mountain.

stem.en: The ground rises 180 metres above the land around it. It is a…

solution.en: Less than 300 m → hill.

html.en: Mountains have snow, hills do not
A mountain rises more than 300 m above the land around it; a hill rises less than 300 m
Mountains are made of rock, hills of soil

stem.en: What is the difference between mountains and hills?

solution.en: It is a number: more than 300 m = mountain, less than 300 m = hill.

stem.en: What are the two main types of maps?

solution.en: Topographic maps and relief maps.

html.en: Only how high the land is
The natural features of the land AND things made by people, such as roads and towns

stem.en: What do topographic maps show?

solution.en: Natural features (hills, mountains, lakes, rivers) and human-made features (roads, towns). Many atlases contain them.

html.en: Only how high the different parts of a region, country or continent are

stem.en: What do relief maps show?

solution.en: Only height. Nothing else.

stem.en: On a map, land areas of the same height above sea level are…

solution.en: They are given the same colour, usually shades of brown and green.

html.en: To show what the different colours and symbols on the map mean

stem.en: What is a map key used for?

solution.en: The key explains what the colours and symbols mean, so you can read the map.

html.en: From the top of the nearest mountain
Above and below the average level of the sea
From the centre of the Earth

stem.en: How are heights and depths measured on a map?

solution.en: Above and below the average level of the sea — "above sea level".

html.en: Above the ground at its base

stem.en: Mount Everest is 8,863 metres high. That means it is 8,863 metres…

solution.en: Above sea level.

html.en: Places that are the same height above sea level

stem.en: What do contour lines show on a map?

solution.en: Lines joining places that are the same height above sea level. They are exactly level.

stem.en: Do contour lines cross each other?

solution.en: Never. If they seem to join up or stop, it is because they have reached a cliff or another vertical surface.

stem.en: Contour lines that are close together mean the slope is…

solution.en: Close together = steep.

stem.en: Contour lines that are far apart mean the slope is…

solution.en: Far apart = gentle.

stem.en: If there are no contour lines at all, the land is…

solution.en: Flat.

stem.en: On a small-scale map in an atlas, contour lines may be at intervals of…

solution.en: 1,000 or 2,000 metres — a small-scale map covers a huge area with little detail.

stem.en: On a large-scale map, contour lines may be at intervals of…

solution.en: 10 metres or even less — a large-scale map shows a small area in lots of detail.

html.en: A small-scale map shows a large area with little detail; a large-scale map shows a small area with lots of detail
A small-scale map is printed smaller
A large-scale map is only used at sea

stem.en: What is the difference between a small-scale and a large-scale map?

solution.en: Small-scale = large area, little detail. Large-scale = small area, lots of detail.

stem.en: The source of a river is…

solution.en: The beginning of a river, usually on high ground.

html.en: The place where it meets a lake or an ocean

stem.en: The mouth of a river is…

solution.en: The end of the river, where it meets a larger body of water.

stem.en: The banks of a river are…

solution.en: The sides. The bottom is the riverbed.

html.en: When the river dries up completely
When the river overflows its banks after heavy rain

stem.en: What is a flood?

solution.en: When, after heavy rain, the river overflows its banks.

stem.en: Areas where a river flows very fast over rocks, dangerous for boats, are called…

solution.en: Rapids.

stem.en: A large area of flat land that is raised higher than the land around it is a…

solution.en: A plateau.

stem.en: A narrow valley with steep sides caused by erosion is a…

solution.en: A canyon.

stem.en: A narrow strip of land that connects two large areas of land is an…

solution.en: An isthmus. A strip that extends out into water is a peninsula.

stem.en: In the water cycle, the sun warming water so it turns into gas is called…

solution.en: Evaporation. From living things it is called transpiration.

stem.en: Water vapour getting cold high in the sky and forming clouds is called…

solution.en: Condensation.

stem.en: Most mountains are found in…

solution.en: Most are in long chains called ranges. Only a few stand alone.

stem.en: Which of these is a mountain that stands alone?

solution.en: Fujiyama. Also Mount Taranaki (New Zealand), Mount Kenya and Kilimanjaro (Africa).

stem.en: Which of these is a mountain range?

solution.en: The Himalayas. Also the Alps, Andes, Sarawat and Rocky Mountains.

stem.en: What is the Earth made up of?

solution.en: Layers of rock. The solid outside layer is the crust; beneath it is the mantle.

stem.en: What is the solid outside layer of rock called?

solution.en: The Earth's crust.

html.en: So hot that they have melted into a thick liquid like sticky tar

stem.en: Near the top of the mantle, the rocks are…

solution.en: They have melted into a thick liquid like sticky tar — molten rock, or magma.

html.en: Large pieces called plates that fit together like a jigsaw puzzle

stem.en: What is the Earth's crust made up of?

solution.en: Large pieces called plates, fitting together like a jigsaw puzzle. Some carry continents, some carry oceans.

html.en: Floating on the molten rock of the mantle below them

stem.en: The plates move because they are…

solution.en: They float on the molten rock of the mantle and move slowly.

html.en: Two plates push together and fold the crust
Molten rock under great pressure bursts through a weak point in the crust onto the surface
Blocks of rock are pushed up between two faults

stem.en: How is a volcanic mountain formed?

solution.en: The rocks press down on the mantle, so the molten rock is under great pressure. At a weak point in the crust it bursts through onto the surface, forming a volcano.

stem.en: Which mountain in Africa is a volcanic mountain that stands alone?

solution.en: Mount Kilimanjaro.

html.en: Where two plates push against each other the crust is slowly pushed up in folds or ridges
Rocks crack into faults and blocks rise

stem.en: How are fold mountains formed?

solution.en: Two plates push against each other → the crust is pushed up into folds or ridges.

stem.en: Which range formed when the plate carrying India moved into the plate carrying Asia?

solution.en: The Himalayas. The rocks in the sea between them were pushed up into folds.

html.en: The rocks that formed the Himalayas used to be under the sea between India and Asia

stem.en: Why can fossilised seashells be found near the tops of the Himalayas?

solution.en: Because the rock was once the seabed between India and Asia, before it was pushed up into folds.

stem.en: Which of these lists contains only fold mountains?

solution.en: The Alps, Rockies, Andes and Urals are all fold mountains, like the Himalayas.

html.en: It gets a few centimetres wider
It gets a few metres narrower

stem.en: What happens to the Atlantic Ocean each year, as Europe and North America move apart?

solution.en: A few centimetres wider every year.

html.en: A break created when rocks crack as they move apart

stem.en: What is a fault?

solution.en: A break in the rock, created when rocks crack as they move apart.

html.en: Magma bursts through a weak point
Large blocks of rock are pushed up between two faults
Two plates push together and fold

stem.en: How are block mountains formed?

solution.en: As plates move apart the rocks crack into faults, and large blocks are pushed up between two faults.

html.en: Some of the highland areas of East Africa

stem.en: Where are the block mountains named in your book?

solution.en: Some of the highland areas of East Africa.

stem.en: Block mountains often have…

solution.en: Flat tops.

stem.en: What is a flat-topped highland called?

solution.en: A plateau.

stem.en: Two plates pushing together creates…

solution.en: Fold mountains. Plates moving apart creates block mountains.

html.en: The distance you can see from a mountain

stem.en: What is a mountain range?

solution.en: A long chain of mountains — the Alps, Andes, Himalayas, Sarawat and Rockies.

html.en: About 5,000–6,000 years ago, in Mesopotamia between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers

stem.en: About how long ago did the first cities appear, and where?

solution.en: About 5,000–6,000 years ago in Mesopotamia. Other early cities grew along the Nile, the Indus and the Yellow River.

html.en: Rivers gave water, food, fertile soil for farming and transport

stem.en: Why did the first cities grow up beside rivers?

solution.en: Water, food, fertile soil and transport — everything a settlement needs.

html.en: Homes, shops, offices, banks, factories, schools, hospitals, stations and civic buildings

stem.en: In most modern cities, land is used for…

solution.en: All of those — plus civic buildings such as city halls or town halls.

html.en: A city hall or town hall

stem.en: What is a civic building?

solution.en: A building for the running of the city, such as a city hall or town hall.

html.en: Because the city has developed over a long period of time

stem.en: Why do many cities have a mixture of older and newer buildings?

solution.en: Because the city has developed over a long period of time.

html.en: Because land in the city centre is very expensive, so building upwards makes the most of the land
Because the ground is stronger there
To be closer to the river

stem.en: Why are skyscrapers built in city centres?

solution.en: Land in the city centre is very expensive, so people build very tall to make the most of the land.

stem.en: Cities may be divided into different areas called…

solution.en: Zones, each with a different purpose.

html.en: The central business district — the middle of the city, where most businesses are

stem.en: What is the CBD?

solution.en: The Central Business District — the centre of the city where most businesses are located.

html.en: Most of the offices, banks, large shops, art galleries and museums

stem.en: What can you find in the CBD?

solution.en: Offices, banks, large shops, art galleries and museums.

html.en: Commuter trains and metros let people live further away and still travel to work

stem.en: How has better transport helped cities to grow outwards?

solution.en: Commuter trains and metros mean people can live further from the centre and still travel to work.

html.en: A person who travels from home to work
A person who lives in the CBD

stem.en: What is a commuter?

solution.en: A person who travels from home to work.

html.en: A residential area on the edge of the city
An industrial zone in the CBD

stem.en: What is a suburb, and where is it?

solution.en: A residential area that develops around the edges of the city.

html.en: One very large urban area formed when neighbouring towns and cities merge

stem.en: What is a conurbation?

solution.en: Neighbouring towns and cities merge and become one very large urban area.

stem.en: Which two cities in Pakistan, originally 13 km apart, joined to form one conurbation?

solution.en: Rawalpindi and Islamabad.

html.en: Tokyo and Yokohama, with 34 million people

stem.en: Which is generally agreed to be the largest conurbation in the world?

solution.en: Tokyo and Yokohama in Japan — about 34 million people.

stem.en: Which are the two largest cities in Australia?

solution.en: Sydney and Melbourne.

stem.en: A disadvantage of living in a conurbation is…

solution.en: Traffic, pollution, crowding, expensive housing and very little green space.

html.en: The biggest city in a country
The city where the government of the country meets
The city with the most factories
The oldest city in a country

stem.en: What is a capital city?

solution.en: Where the government of the country meets. It is usually — but not always — the largest and most important city.

html.en: To be the centre of government, where laws are made and the leaders work

stem.en: What is the main purpose of a capital city?

solution.en: It is the centre of government.

html.en: Because people could not decide between Sydney and Melbourne, so a new capital was built
Because it is on the coast
Because it was the biggest city

stem.en: Why was Canberra built?

solution.en: The people could not decide between Sydney and Melbourne, so they built a new city to be the capital.

html.en: Inland, about halfway between Sydney and Melbourne, in 1927

stem.en: Where is Canberra, and when did it become the capital?

solution.en: Inland, about halfway between Sydney and Melbourne. It became the capital in 1927.

stem.en: Which of these is a specially-built capital city?

solution.en: Brasília. Others are Islamabad, Abuja, New Delhi and Canberra.

stem.en: The capital of Brazil is…

solution.en: Brasília — a classic exam trap.

stem.en: The capital of Bolivia is…

solution.en: Sucre is the one listed in your booklet.

stem.en: The capital of Argentina is…

solution.en: Buenos Aires.

stem.en: The capital of Peru is…

solution.en: Lima.

stem.en: The capital of Ecuador is…

solution.en: Quito.

stem.en: The capital of Colombia is…

solution.en: Bogotá.

stem.en: The capital of Venezuela is…

solution.en: Caracas.

stem.en: The capital of Chile is…

solution.en: Santiago.

stem.en: The capital of Uruguay is…

solution.en: Montevideo. Asunción is Paraguay.

stem.en: The capital of Guyana is…

solution.en: Georgetown. Suriname is Paramaribo, French Guiana is Cayenne.

stem.en: The capital of the Falkland Islands is…

solution.en: Stanley.

stem.en: The equator passes through which South American countries?

solution.en: Ecuador, Colombia and Brazil.

stem.en: The capital of Canada is…

solution.en: Ottawa.

stem.en: The capital of Mexico is…

solution.en: Mexico City.

stem.en: The capital of Cuba is…

solution.en: Havana.

stem.en: North America is the ___ largest continent.

solution.en: The third largest. Bordered north by the Arctic Ocean, east by the Atlantic, west and south by the Pacific.

stem.en: The capital of Switzerland is…

solution.en: Bern — not Zurich or Geneva.

stem.en: The capital of Turkey is…

solution.en: Ankara — not Istanbul.

stem.en: The capital of Germany is…

solution.en: Berlin.

stem.en: The capital of Spain is…

solution.en: Madrid. Lisbon is Portugal.

stem.en: The capital of Wales is…

solution.en: Cardiff. Scotland is Edinburgh, Ireland is Dublin.

stem.en: Great Britain consists of which three countries?

solution.en: England, Scotland and Wales. Those three plus Northern Ireland are the United Kingdom.

stem.en: The capital of Nigeria, which was specially built, is…

solution.en: Abuja — Lagos is bigger, but Abuja is the capital.

text.en: 🏞️ Read Amazon River. Learn the 6 headline facts (source, mouth, length, countries, volume, rainforest). Then Practice + Label the river.
🛢️ Read River Pollution. Do Cause / Damage / Cure and build acid rain in order twice.
🗺️ Read Mountains, Rivers and Hills. Play the whole Map Lab: contour lines, slopes, relief map.
🌋 Read How Are Mountains Formed. Run all three animations in the Mountain Lab and say each one out loud.
🏙️ Read The Growth of Cities + 🏛️ Capital Cities. Practice both, then the capital match for all three continents.
⏱️ Full Mock Exam. Review every mistake, then re-practise only those topics.

html.en:
🗓️ A 6-day plan to be ready

Short sessions beat one long panic session. 25–35 minutes a day is plenty.

⭐ The marks students throw away every year

  1. Forgetting the number: more than 300 m = mountain, less than 300 m = hill.
  2. Saying contour lines show "the shape of the hill". They join places of the same height above sea level.
  3. Saying contour lines close together = gentle. Close together = steep. Far apart = gentle. None at all = flat.
  4. Mixing up topographic maps (natural and human-made features) with relief maps (only height).
  5. Saying the Earth's crust is made of "rocks". It is made of large pieces called plates that fit together like a jigsaw.
  6. Saying fold mountains form when plates move apart. Fold = push together. Block = move apart and crack into faults.
  7. Forgetting that a flat-topped highland is called a plateau.
  8. In acid rain, forgetting to name the gas. It is sulphur dioxide (and other gases).
  9. Saying acid rain falls where the gas was made. It can fall hundreds of kilometres away.
  10. Listing only "rubbish" as a cause of river pollution. There are four: sewage, chemical waste, farm chemicals, waste oil and rubbish.
  11. Saying the source is where the river ends. Source = start. Mouth = where it meets the sea or a lake.
  12. Saying the capital is always the biggest city. It is where the government meets — it is usually, not always, the biggest (Canberra, Brasília, Abuja).
  13. Writing "Rio de Janeiro" for Brazil. It is Brasília. And Bolivia's is Sucre.
  14. Leaving a question blank. Always write something.
The night before: don't learn anything new. Re-read the blue rule boxes in Learn, do 10 quick questions in Practice, then stop. Sleep is worth more marks than another hour of studying. 😴

In the exam: read every question twice. Underline the question word (name, describe, explain, why, how). If it says explain, write a because… sentence. If it says name two, write two — not one, not three. If it says give 3 examples, count them on your fingers before you move on. ✍️
